title: Distinct Subsequences
hints: think of building t one character at a time by scanning through s - at each position in s, you either use that character toward matching t, or skip it entirely
define dp[i][j] as the number of distinct ways the first i characters of s can form the first j characters of t
you can always skip s[i-1] and keep looking: that contributes dp[i-1][j] ways
if s[i-1] == t[j-1], you can also choose to use s[i-1] to match t[j-1], contributing dp[i-1][j-1] more ways, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]
base case: dp[i][0] = 1 for all i (there's exactly one way to form an empty t, by using none of s), and dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0 (an empty s can't form a non-empty t)
commonMistakes: forgetting that dp[i][0] should be 1 for every i, not 0, since matching an empty target always has exactly one (trivial) way
only adding dp[i-1][j-1] when characters match and forgetting to also carry forward dp[i-1][j] (the option to skip s[i-1])
confusing this with longest common subsequence and taking a max instead of summing counts

content.problemStatement:
You're given two strings, `s` and `t`. A subsequence is formed by deleting
some (possibly zero) characters from `s` without reordering the rest; two
ways are counted separately if they use different positions of `s`, even
if the resulting characters look the same.

**Count the number of distinct ways that `t` appears as a subsequence of `s`.**
constraints: s and t consist of English letters
the answer fits within a 32-bit signed integer for the given bounds
notes: t is longer than s (answer is always 0)
t is empty (there is exactly one way, the empty subsequence)
s and t are identical (exactly one way)
s has many repeated characters that all match a single character of t

sampleTestCases.explanation: There are 3 distinct ways to pick positions in "rabbbit" that spell out "rabbit", each choosing a different one of the three b's to drop.
t is longer than s, so t cannot possibly be a subsequence of s.
